content:
There is no single shoe that suits everyone with arthritis. Start with the fit of your own feet and the activity you want to do. A shoe should hold your foot securely without squeezing painful joints. This is a features-based guide, not a tested product ranking. We have not tested or ranked brands, and this guide contains no affiliate links.

Which features are worth trying?

NHS Bristol, North Somerset and South Gloucestershire footwear advice stresses that footwear needs vary with foot shape, pain and activity. Its suggestions are starting points for trying shoes, not a prescription for every type of arthritis.

  • Space around the toes: check length, width and depth. Toes should not be compressed against the front, sides or upper. Extra width alone may not make room above a raised toe joint.
  • A secure fit: adjustable laces or straps can hold the foot without relying on your toes to grip the shoe. Choose a fastening you can manage with your hands.
  • Comfort around painful areas: check seams and stiff edges over bunions or prominent joints. A softer upper may reduce pressure there.
  • A stable base: a broad heel and a sole with grip are useful features to assess. Try the shoe while standing and walking, rather than judging it by its appearance.
  • Room for prescribed insoles: a removable liner can help make space, but it is not essential for everyone. Bring your insoles to the fitting and follow the prescriber's advice.

Sole stiffness needs individual judgement. Some people with painful forefoot joints benefit from a stiffer or curved rocker sole, while others need a different design. Do not use a twist test or a fixed heel height as a universal rule. Ask a podiatrist or orthotist if a change in sole design affects your balance or walking. NHS Ayrshire & Arran's footwear guidance describes support, fit and rocker soles in more detail.

How can you check the fit?

Try both shoes with the socks and any prescribed insoles you intend to use. Check both feet, including while standing. The NHS Bristol, North Somerset and South Gloucestershire guide suggests about 1 cm of space beyond the longest toe, but length is only one part of fit. Your heel should not repeatedly slip and the shoe should not leave your toes cramped.

Walk a short distance somewhere safe. Check for rubbing, pressure over joints and difficulty keeping the shoe on. If your feet swell during the day, try shoes when that swelling is usually present. Do not buy an ordinary retail pair that hurts on the assumption that it will stretch to fit. Prescribed adapted footwear is different: follow your orthotist's gradual wearing-in plan and ask the service about persistent discomfort.

For work, uneven paths or exercise, check the demands of that setting too. A comfortable indoor shoe is not necessarily suitable for wet ground or a workplace with protective-footwear requirements.

Does the type of arthritis change the advice?

Osteoarthritis and insoles

NICE NG226, recommendation 1.3.11, says not to routinely offer insoles, braces, tape, splints or supports for osteoarthritis unless all three conditions apply:

  1. there is joint instability or abnormal biomechanical loading;
  2. therapeutic exercise is ineffective or unsuitable without adding an aid or device; and
  3. the aid or device is likely to improve movement and function.

This is guidance about clinical use of devices. It is not a NICE ranking of retail shoes, and it does not mean everyone must fail an exercise course before an aid can be considered. Recommendations 1.3.1 to 1.3.4 support exercise tailored to the person, including strengthening and aerobic fitness. Discuss persistent pain or difficulty exercising with your clinician.

Rheumatoid arthritis

NICE NG100, recommendations 1.8.5 and 1.8.6, says adults with rheumatoid arthritis and foot problems should have access to podiatry assessment and periodic review. Functional insoles and therapeutic footwear should be available when indicated. This is not an automatic prescription for any particular shoe or a promise about local waiting times. Ask your rheumatology team how to access assessment.

Bunions and a painful big toe

For bunions, the NHS recommends wide shoes with a low heel and soft sole, avoiding high heels and tight, pointed shoes. A bunion and a stiff arthritic big toe are not the same problem. If your big toe does not bend comfortably, ask whether a sole modification is appropriate rather than buying a rocker shoe solely on an online claim.

New pain or swelling

A larger shoe does not explain or treat new swelling. A suddenly hot, swollen joint could need urgent assessment, including when you have previously had gout. Use the urgent-help advice below rather than assuming this is a footwear problem.

When is a foot assessment useful?

Ask for advice if changes in foot shape, recurring rubbing or pain make ordinary shoes difficult to wear. Mention reduced sensation, diabetes, circulation problems or wounds rather than treating these as fitting issues alone. Your GP surgery, rheumatology team or local podiatry service can explain referral or self-referral arrangements. Access routes and eligibility vary locally.

An orthotics assessment may lead to insoles, changes to existing footwear or specialist footwear, depending on the problem. Guy's and St Thomas' describes prescribed footwear adaptations; it is an example of an NHS service, not a UK-wide entitlement to a particular product.

Can shoes replace exercise or arthritis treatment?

No. Comfortable footwear can make activity more manageable, but it does not replace treatment of inflammatory arthritis or a tailored exercise plan. Ask your physiotherapist to help adapt activity if foot pain limits it. Do not stop prescribed arthritis medicines because footwear feels helpful.

Our foot and ankle arthritis guide explains the condition in more detail. Linked guides are further reading, not evidence that each has received a separate clinical review.

Buying without paying for unsupported promises

This guide does not identify a best brand or price point. Be cautious about products advertised as curing arthritis or correcting every cause of knee or back pain. Ask what the proposed feature is meant to do for your particular foot problem.

Before buying, check how you may try the shoes and whether a change-of-mind return is allowed. GOV.UK explains the difference between shop and distance purchases. A shop does not generally have to accept a non-faulty change-of-mind return. For most online orders, you have 14 days after receipt to tell the seller you want to cancel, then another 14 days to return the goods. Exceptions include personalised or custom-made items. Faulty-goods rights are separate. Check the terms before ordering specialist footwear or wearing a pair outdoors.

When should you get medical help?

Seek urgent assessment, even without a fever, for sudden severe joint pain, difficulty moving or bearing weight on the joint, or a hot, swollen joint, with or without a colour change. NHS septic arthritis advice explains that not everyone with a joint infection has a fever. Do not wait for shoe changes to help.

After an injury, severe joint pain, inability to walk or put weight on a joint, or a joint that has moved out of place needs A&E assessment. See NHS joint pain advice.

NHS swelling advice also calls for urgent help for unexplained swelling in one foot, ankle or leg, or swelling that is sudden, severe, painful, red or hot. In England, Scotland and Wales, contact an urgent GP service or call 111. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service.

If you have diabetes and develop a new sore, skin break, hot swollen foot, change of shape or new foot pain, contact your podiatry or GP team urgently. NHS inform's diabetic foot advice says a foot turning very pale or blue, especially with new numbness or pain, needs 999 or A&E.

Call 999 if pain and swelling in a leg are accompanied by chest pain or shortness of breath. These can be signs of a clot in the lungs. Do not drive yourself. See NHS DVT advice.

For persistent, worsening or recurring foot pain without urgent signs, arrange a GP or podiatry assessment. The NHS foot pain hub links to advice for different parts of the foot.

Frequently asked questions

Are there NICE-approved shoes for arthritis?

The NICE guidance cited here addresses osteoarthritis devices and rheumatoid arthritis foot care. It does not rank retail shoe brands. Use fit and an assessment of your needs, not an implied NICE endorsement.

Does every shoe need a removable insole?

No. It can be useful if you need space for prescribed orthoses, but fit and your own treatment plan matter more than a universal checklist.

Can I get footwear on the NHS?

Specialist footwear or adaptations may be offered after assessment. For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE says therapeutic footwear should be available if indicated. Ask your local team about the pathway and your needs; this guide cannot confirm eligibility or stock.

Should I keep wearing shoes that rub?

For ordinary retail shoes, do not assume rubbing will disappear with use. For prescribed adapted footwear, follow the wearing-in instructions from your orthotist. Ask about persistent pressure areas, and get urgent help for new foot damage if you have diabetes.

General UK information, not an individual diagnosis or footwear prescription. Follow advice from the team looking after your feet. For urgent symptoms, use the services described above.
